New prediction market traders and readers of The Post can qualify for the Polymarket promo code NYPMAX1 to deposit $10, to get a $25 trading bonus for any Week 13 game on Saturday’s college football card.

Rivalry week is here, and there are several high-profile clashes that await us, including Alabama vs. Auburn, Michigan vs. Ohio State, and USC vs. UCLA.

Enter the Polymarket promo code NYPMAX1 when you sign up and deposit $10 to receive a $25 trading bonus.

New users can use their $25 bonus to trade on the market of their choice.

You can gain instant access to the Polymarket mobile app by using the Polymarket promo code NYPMAX1:

The Polymarket promo is available to eligible new users who reside in Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Wisconsin, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

The College Football Playoff picture has come into focus, but there is still plenty of time for chaos.

Auburn would love nothing more than to spoil Alabama’s season, while USC will relish the chance to give UCLA something to think about before the big dance.

18+ Only. Restrictions and eligibility requirements apply. Not available in all jurisdictions. Trading is risky. 100% loss can occur. See polymarket.com/tos for more information. The Polymarket US App serves as an independent software provider and affiliate of Polymarket US and Polymarket Clearing, the CFTC-regulated exchange and clearing organization.

news.content: در نتایج جستجوی خود، پوشش خبری بیشتر ما را مشاهده کنید. معامله‌گران جدید بازار پیش‌بینی و خوانندگان The Post می‌توانند واجد شرایط استفاده از کد تخفیف Polymarket با عنوان NYPMAX1 شوند تا با واریز 10 دلار، 25 دلار پاداش معاملاتی برای هر بازی هفته 13 در برنامه فوتبال دانشگاهی روز شنبه دریافت کنند. هفته رقابت فرا رسیده است و چندین بازی مهم در انتظار ما هستند، از جمله آلاباما در مقابل آبرن، میشیگان در مقابل ایالت اوهایو و USC در مقابل UCLA. هنگام ثبت‌نام، کد تبلیغاتی Polymarket یعنی NYPMAX1 را وارد کرده و 10 دلار واریز کنید تا 25 دلار بونوس معاملاتی دریافت کنید. کاربران جدید می‌توانند از بونوس 25 دلاری خود برای معامله در بازار انتخابی‌شان استفاده کنند. با استفاده از کد تبلیغاتی Polymarket یعنی NYPMAX1 می‌توانید فوراً به اپلیکیشن موبایل Polymarket دسترسی پیدا کنید: تبلیغات Polymarket برای کاربران جدید واجد شرایطی که در آلاسکا، آلاباما، آرکانزاس، کالیفرنیا، کلرادو، کنتیکت، ناحیه کلمبیا، دلاور، فلوریدا، جورجیا، هاوایی، آیووا، آیداهو، ایندیانا، کانزاس، کنتاکی، لوئیزیانا، مین، مینه سوتا، میسوری، می سی سی پی، کارولینای شمالی، داکوتای شمالی، نبراسکا، نیوهمپشایر، نیوجرسی، نیومکزیکو، نیویورک، اوکلاهما، اورگان، پنسیلوانیا، رود آیلند، کارولینای جنوبی، داکوتای جنوبی، تنسی تصویر پلی‌آف فوتبال کالج در کانون توجه قرار گرفته است، اما هنوز زمان زیادی برای آشفتگی وجود دارد. آبرن هیچ چیز را بیشتر از خراب کردن فصل آلاباما دوست ندارد، در حالی که USC از فرصتی برای دادن چیزی به UCLA برای فکر کردن قبل از رقابت بزرگ لذت خواهد برد. فقط افراد بالای 18 سال. محدودیت‌ها اعمال می‌شود

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Mississippi woman is sharing a shocking dating story online — and it’s either silly or sinister, depending on whom you trust.

“You won’t believe what happened to me,” said Maranda Joiner, a speaker and leadership strategist based in Jackson, in a recent TikTok post.

Joiner said she met a man at a music festival and, after a handful of breezy lunch dates—none of which included intimacy of any kind or, in Joiner’s estimation, a spark— their communication dwindled.

When the man reached out to ask why she’d gone dark, Joiner told him it wasn’t the connection she was hoping for, and she’d started dating other people.

Undeterred — and absolutely unhinged — the man messaged back offering a gift.

“His wording is important,” said Joiner. “He said, ‘I have a gift for you. Something that I think you’ll like just because.'”

But Joiner wondered why he was buying gifts for her at all — they were, after all, kaput.

The strange suitor explained that he had purchased the gift when they went to lunch and didn’t know Joiner was “going to curve” him so quickly.

“He says, ‘It’s just something I think you should have, and you deserve it.’ Key words: You deserve it.“

A few days later, Joiner messaged the man to say she was going to the mall and he could bring her the gift at Dillard’s.

Eerily, the man said he was already at Dillard’s.

(Cue the horror soundtrack.)

Once Joiner arrived at the department store, the spurned date approached her with a blue-and-white gift bag and, after making small talk, interrupted to ask if she would open the gift.

“I said, ‘Oh, OK, sure, I’ll open the gift.’ And all the money in the world. I’m betting that you’re not gonna be able to guess what I’m about to pull out of this bag.”

The gift? A poseable doll with her face on it, wearing an outfit she’d sported in a recent social media post.

“Sir, is this a voodoo doll?” she asked him. “Do you have more of these?!”

Allegedly, the man was simply confounded that Joiner didn’t appreciate the hex-y present, suggesting she could display it on her desk at work.

“I’m not putting this in my office!” she insisted, asking whether the doll contained a tracking device.

“I’m gonna burn it and probably stop dating for a while,” she concluded.

The comments section was, understandably, appalled and expressed concern for Joiner’s safety.

“Change your routines. That man has been stalking you,” recommended one commenter.

“In the words of [“Ghost” psychic] Oda Mae Brown, ‘You in danger girl,'” said another.

“You’ve come across a warlock, block him,” urged a third.

“He is obsessed, diabolical, and very dangerous,” stressed a fourth.

Many commenters were so shaken, they even recommended that Joiner seek spiritual protection through prayer, fasting or the intervention of a priest or practiced healer.

One commenter offered another kind of prayer that seems to capture the lesson of this story:

“Baby, let me stay single.”
news.content:
در نتایج جستجوی خود، اخبار بیشتری از ما را مشاهده کنید. یک زن اهل میسیسیپی در حال اشتراک‌گذاری یک داستان تکان‌دهنده درباره قرار ملاقات آنلاین است — و بسته به اینکه به چه کسی اعتماد دارید، این داستان یا احمقانه است یا شوم.ماراندا جوینر، سخنران و استراتژیست رهبری مستقر در جکسون، در یک پست اخیر در TikTok گفت: «باور نمی‌کنید چه اتفاقی برای من افتاد.» جوイナー گفت که در یک جشنواره موسیقی با مردی آشنا شد و پس از چند قرار ناهار سبک - که هیچ‌کدام شامل صمیمیت از هیچ نوعی یا به قول جوイナー، هیچ جرقه‌ای نبود - ارتباط آنها کمرنگ شد. وقتی مرد با او تماس گرفت تا بپرسد چرا دیگر خبری از او نیست، جوイナー به او گفت که این ارتباطی نیست که او انتظارش را داشته و شروع به قرار گذاشتن با افراد دیگر کرده است. مرد که ناامید نشده بود - و کاملاً از کوره در رفته بود - در پاسخ پیامی فرستاد و هدیه‌ای پیشنهاد کرد. جوイナー گفت: «نحوه بیان او مهم است. «او گفت: «یک هدیه برایت دارم. چیزی که فکر می‌کنم فقط به این دلیل خوشت بیاید.»
اما جوینر تعجب کرد که چرا اصلاً برای او هدیه می‌خرد — بالاخره رابطه‌شان تمام شده بود. این خواستگار عجیب توضیح داد که وقتی برای ناهار بیرون رفته بودند، هدیه را خریده بود و نمی‌دانست که جوینر اینقدر زود «او را رد خواهد کرد».او گفت: «فقط چیزیه که فکر می‌کنم باید داشته باشی و لیاقتش رو داری. ’ کلمات کلیدی: تو لایقش هستی.»
چند روز بعد، جوینر به مرد پیام داد و گفت که قصد دارد به مرکز خرید برود و او می‌تواند هدیه را در فروشگاه دیلاردز به او بدهد. به طرز عجیبی، مرد گفت که از قبل در دیلاردز بوده است.(موسیقی متن فیلم ترسناک پخش شود.)
وقتی Joiner به فروشگاه رسید، مردی که از او خواستگاری کرده بود و Joiner او را رد کرده بود، نزدیک شد.

منبع تصویر، AFP via Getty Images

جعفر ماهر اوغلو، مالک شبکه خبری «خلق تی‌وی» ترکیه که در لندن اقامت دارد، به بی‌بی‌سی گفت که مقام‌های ترکیه یکی از پربیننده‌ترین شبکه‌های خبری این کشور را «نابود» کرده‌اند.

آقای ماهر اوغلو در گفت‌وگو با برنامه خبری سرویس جهانی بی‌بی‌سی گفت که تنها در هفته جاری ۹ نفر از افراد مرتبط با خلق تی‌وی به اتهاماتی از جمله پولشویی، رشوه‌خواری و انتشار اطلاعات گمراه‌کننده بازداشت شدند.

او گفت که چندین نفر از اعضای خانواده‌اش نیز در میان کسانی بودند که ماه گذشته، همزمان با به دست گرفتن کنترل این شبکه حامی مخالفان از سوی دولت، بازداشت شدند. او اتهامات علیه خود و این شبکه تلویزیونی را «کاملا نادرست» خواند.

دادستانی کل استانبول اعلام کرد که دو تن از مجریان سابق بخش خبری این شبکه در میان تازه‌ترین بازداشت‌شدگان هستند.

مقام‌های قضایی ترکیه در بیانیه‌ای این مجریان را به تهیه «گزارش‌های نادرست» در ازای دریافت پول متهم کردند.

بر اساس این بیانیه، مقام‌های ترکیه همچنین حکم بازداشت کورشاد اوغوز، هماهنگ‌کننده بخش خبر این شبکه را صادر کرده‌اند که در خارج از کشور به سر می‌برد. در این بیانیه به محل اقامت او اشاره‌ای نشده است.

آقای ماهر اوغلو به بی‌بی‌سی گفت که در صورت بازگشت به ترکیه ممکن است روانه زندان شود.

او گفت: «[دولت] می‌خواهد که کنترل تمام رسانه‌ها را در دست داشته باشد... من بیش از آنکه نگران شبکه‌ام باشم، نگران کشورم و دموکراسی آن هستم.»

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

ماه گذشته مقام‌های ترکیه با یورش به دفتر مرکزی شبکه «خلق تی‌وی» (Halk TV)، پخش زنده برنامه‌های آن را متوقف کردند. این اقدام تازه‌ترین مورد از سلسله اقدامات سرکوبگرانه علیه رسانه‌هایی است که منتقد رجب طیب اردوغان، رئیس‌جمهور ترکیه و دولت او شناخته می‌شوند.

دولت ترکیه پس از آن مدیر جدیدی برای اداره این شبکه منصوب کرد.

دولت آقای اردوغان بخش عمده‌ای از رسانه‌های ترکیه را در کنترل خود دارد و آن کشور از نظر آزادی مطبوعات در شمار کشورهای دارای بدترین وضعیت در جهان قرار دارد. با این حال، دولت ترکیه تاکید دارد که کارکنان رسانه‌ها را به دلیل فعالیت‌های روزنامه‌نگاری بازداشت نمی‌کند.

آقای اردوغان از زمان پیروزی با اختلاف اندک در انتخابات ریاست‌جمهوری سال ۲۰۲۳، سرکوب مخالفان را تشدید کرده است.

اوایل ماه جاری میلادی نیز مقام‌های ترکیه کنترل شبکه «سوزجو تی‌وی» (Sözcü TV)، از دیگر شبکه‌های تلویزیونی حامی مخالفان دولت، را در دست گرفتند.

اکرم امام‌اوغلو، شهردار استانبول و رقیب اصلی آقای اردوغان، به اتهام فساد و نقض قوانین انتخاباتی زندانی شده است؛ اتهاماتی که او و حزبش به‌شدت رد کرده‌اند.

صدها نفر از هواداران آقای امام‌اوغلو نیز با اتهامات مشابهی روبه‌رو شده‌اند. دولت ترکیه همچنین شماری دیگر از فعالان، وکلا و کمدین‌ها را روانه زندان کرده است.

ماه گذشته مقام‌های ترکیه با یورش به دفتر مرکزی شبکه «خلق تی‌وی» (Halk TV)، پخش زنده برنامه‌های آن را متوقف کردند. این اقدام تازه‌ترین مورد از سلسله اقدامات سرکوبگرانه علیه رسانه‌هایی است که منتقد رجب طیب اردوغان، رئیس‌جمهور ترکیه و دولت او شناخته می‌شوند.

دولت ترکیه پس از آن مدیر جدیدی برای اداره این شبکه منصوب کرد.

دولت آقای اردوغان بخش عمده‌ای از رسانه‌های ترکیه را در کنترل خود دارد و آن کشور از نظر آزادی مطبوعات در شمار کشورهای دارای بدترین وضعیت در جهان قرار دارد. با این حال، دولت ترکیه تاکید دارد که کارکنان رسانه‌ها را به دلیل فعالیت‌های روزنامه‌نگاری بازداشت نمی‌کند.

آقای اردوغان از زمان پیروزی با اختلاف اندک در انتخابات ریاست‌جمهوری سال ۲۰۲۳، سرکوب مخالفان را تشدید کرده است.

اوایل ماه جاری میلادی نیز مقام‌های ترکیه کنترل شبکه «سوزجو تی‌وی» (Sözcü TV)، از دیگر شبکه‌های تلویزیونی حامی مخالفان دولت، را در دست گرفتند.

اکرم امام‌اوغلو، شهردار استانبول و رقیب اصلی آقای اردوغان، به اتهام فساد و نقض قوانین انتخاباتی زندانی شده است؛ اتهاماتی که او و حزبش به‌شدت رد کرده‌اند.

صدها نفر از هواداران آقای امام‌اوغلو نیز با اتهامات مشابهی روبه‌رو شده‌اند. دولت ترکیه همچنین شماری دیگر از فعالان، وکلا و کمدین‌ها را روانه زندان کرده است.

Alan Ruck was honest about his old pal Charlie Sheen’s struggles with sobriety.

“Charlie, over the years, has chosen to wrestle with his demons in the town square and send out invitations,” he told Page Six at the A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s Gala earlier this month.

Ruck and Sheen first met when they co-starred in the 1987 movie “Three for the Road.” The two reunited when Sheen starred in “Spin City” for two seasons after Michael J. Fox was forced to leave the sitcom over his Parkinson’s symptoms.

The “Succession” alum, 70, says that “Charlie was in a good spot when we were doing ‘Spin City.'”

“He was clean and sober,” he explained before gushing over his love for the 61-year-old “Two and a Half Men” alum, calling him someone who “would give you the shirt off his back.”

“I know he’s been sober for a few years again,” he continued about Sheen, who has been sober for the last nine years. “I love the guy. I’m so happy he’s doing well.”

Sheen laid bare his wild times in the 2025 Netflix docuseries “aka Charlie Sheen,” alongside his memoir, “The Book of Sheen,” which explored his struggles with addiction and his HIV diagnosis.

The “Wall Street” star revealed he had a near-fatal cocaine overdose in 1998 and seven stints in rehab.

In a 2025 interview, Sheen confessed that a Mexican drug cartel refused to sell him any more cocaine because they believed he was trafficking it.

news.content:
در نتایج جستجوی خود، پوشش خبری بیشتری از ما را مشاهده کنید. آلن راک در مورد مشکلات دوست قدیمی‌اش چارلی شین در زمینه ترک اعتیاد صادق بود.او اوایل این ماه در مراسم «اتفاق خنده‌داری در مسیر درمان پارکینسون افتاد» به Page Six گفت: «چارلی در طول سال‌ها تصمیم گرفته است که با شیاطین خود در میدان شهر مبارزه کند و دعوت‌نامه‌ها را ارسال کند.» راک و شین اولین بار زمانی که در فیلم «سه نفر برای یک سفر» در سال 1987 نقش‌های اصلی را بازی کردند، با هم آشنا شدند. این دو زمانی دوباره با هم همکاری کردند که شین به مدت دو فصل در «شهر چرخش» بازی کرد؛ این اتفاق پس از آن افتاد که مایکل جی. فاکس به دلیل علائم بیماری پارکینسون مجبور شد سریال کمدی موقعیت را ترک کند. بازیگر سابق «جانشینی»، 70 ساله، می‌گوید که «وقتی ما در حال ساخت «شهر چرخش» بودیم، چارلی در شرایط خوبی قرار داشت.»
او قبل از اینکه از عشقش به بازیگر 61 ساله سریال «دو مرد و نیم» ابراز احساسات کند، توضیح داد: «او پاک و هوشیار بود» و او را کسی خواند که «پیراهن تنش را هم به شما می‌دهد.» او در مورد شین که طی نه سال گذشته هوشیار بوده است، ادامه داد: «می‌دانم که او دوباره چند سالی است که هوشیار بوده است.» «من عاشق این آدم هستم. خیلی خوشحالم که حالش خوب است.»
شین در سریال مستند «aka Charlie Sheen» محصول سال ۲۰۲۵ نتفلیکس، دوران پرفراز و نشیب خود را آشکار کرد. همچنین در کنار این سریال، کتاب خاطراتش با عنوان «کتاب شین» منتشر شد که در آن به بررسی مشکلاتش با اعتیاد و تشخیص بیماری HIV پرداخته است. ستاره «وال استریت» فاش کرد که در سال 1998 تقریباً به دلیل مصرف بیش از حد کوکائین جان خود را از دست داده و هفت بار در مراکز ترک اعتیاد بستری شده است. شین در مصاحبه‌ای در سال 2025 اعتراف کرد که یک کارتل مواد مخدر مکزیکی از فروش بیشتر کوکائین به او خودداری کرده است، زیرا آنها معتقد بودند که او در حال قاچاق کوکائین است. روز خود را با Page آغاز کنید

The Post’s experts pick every game against the spread for Week 12 of the NFL season

Through the first five games of Week 12, several Post experts nailed their bets.

The Post’s Dave Blezow and Drew Loftis went 4-1 against the spread, with the only losses coming on the Lions of Blezow and Packers for Loftis.

On the week, The Post’s Mark Cannizzaro went with 11 favorites compared to five underdogs, the most of any player on the board this week.

Meanwhile, The Post’s Howie Kussoy and Brian Costello took 10 underdogs.

The Patriots to cover +1.5 was unanimous among The Post’s experts, but that line has since flipped with Justin Herbert ruled out due to a concussion.

Another interesting showdown will be Loftis taking the Dolphins +3.5 as a best bet against four other players who have the Jets -3.5 as a best bet.

news.originalContent:
India limp to 116-6 at stumps on day two of the second Test, in reply to the Black Caps’ first innings 356.

India fumbled their chances with bat and ball as a clinical New Zealand finished day two of the second Test well on top, with their pace bowlers shining in the Christchurch sun on Saturday.

India ⁠were 116-6 at stumps in reply to the Black Caps’ first innings 356, with Dhruv Jurel on seven not out and tailender Akash Deep next in the line of fire after Washington Sundar’s dismissal for 10 wrapped up play.

It was ⁠a formidable display by the home quicks, who shared the wickets around and had the ball swinging wildly on a tricky Hagley Oval pitch.

Kyle Jamieson and Jacob Duffy grabbed two wickets apiece, with Nathan Smith and Matt Henry each chipping in another.

Smith landed a hammer blow with the final ball of the day, having Sundar edge a short ball to captain Tom Latham in the slips, ending ‌a tortured, 60-ball knock.

India’s hopes of remaining in contention for the World Test Championship final were already on a knife-edge. They may now be doomed.

Only victory will keep them in the hunt, and that looks far-fetched after a day of poor fielding and squandered starts with the bat.

After dropping Latham on 29 on day one and seeing the opener go on to score 59, India spilled another four catches in the innings after winning the toss and sending the Black Caps in to bat.

Wicketkeeper Tom Blundell, dropped on 49 in the gully, finished with his team’s top score of 89 before ⁠top-edging a Gurnoor Brar delivery to be caught at long leg.

India pacer Akash Deep saw three ⁠chances grassed before he could finally celebrate a five-wicket haul when tailender Henry was caught slogging.

Deep’s 5-99 was a rare highlight for India in the field, with pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah frustrated and wicketless.

India piled on 720-9 in one innings in the drawn first test in Wellington but their top-order batters squandered their starts in Christchurch.

Henry struck with the sixth ball to remove opener Yashasvi Jaiswal for a duck before towering quick Jamieson had number three Devdutt Padikkal caught behind for 21.

Jamieson’s ⁠steepling bounce also knocked over captain Shubman Gill, who edged to the slips ⁠to be out for 17.

A charging Pant tried to seize back control from the bowlers with typical aggression but threw his wicket away for 23 with a big swing at Duffy.

KL Rahul then suffered a moment of madness as he got down on one knee and sliced a drive straight to Devon Conway at ‌point to be out for 25.

Jurel, whose seven runs were eked out of 45 deliveries, and Sundar held on for some 90 minutes in the final session but could barely nudge the score forward.

With New Zealand’s tail-end batters contributing a handy 66 ‌runs ‌between them, Gill will desperately hope for the same lower-order starch from India on day three.

It may still do little to prevent a big New Zealand lead and a platform for the hosts to take a series-sealing victory.
news.content: در پاسخ به امتیاز 356 دور اول بلک‌کپس، هند در پایان روز دوم تست دوم با امتیاز 116-6 در وضعیت بدی قرار دارد. هند شانس‌های خود را با بات و توپ از دست داد و نیوزیلند با عملکردی عالی روز دوم تست دوم را در موقعیت برتری به پایان رساند، در حالی که بولرهای سریع آنها روز شنبه در زیر آفتاب کرایست‌چرچ خوش درخشیدند. در پاسخ به امتیاز 356 اینینگ اول بلک‌کپس، هند در پایان روز اول 116-6 بود، در حالی که درو جورل هفت امتیاز داشت و اوت نشده بود و آکاش دیپ، باتر آخر، پس از اوت شدن واشنگتن سوندار با 10 امتیاز، نفر بعدی بود که به میدان می‌آمد. این نمایش فوق‌العاده‌ای از سوی بولرهای سریع میزبان بود که بین خودشان ویکت‌ها را تقسیم کردند و توپ را در زمین دشوار هگلی اوال به شدت سوئینگ می‌کردند. کایل جیمسون و جیکوب دافی هر کدام دو ویکت گرفتند و ناتان اسمیت و مت هنری هر کدام یک ویکت دیگر گرفتند. اسمیت با آخرین توپ روز یک ضربه کوبنده وارد کرد و باعث شد ساندر یک توپ کوتاه را به سمت کاپیتان تام لاتام در منطقه اسلیپ‌ها لبه کند و به یک ضربه 60 توپی پرفشار پایان دهد. امیدهای هند برای باقی ماندن در رقابت برای فینال قهرمانی جهانی تست از قبل در حد تعادل بود. حالا ممکن است محکوم به شکست باشند. تنها پیروزی می‌تواند آنها را در کورس رقابت نگه دارد و پس از یک روز فیلدینگ ضعیف و شروع‌های ناموفق با چوب، این امر دور از دسترس به نظر می‌رسد. پس از اینکه در روز اول لاتهام را در امتیاز 29 رها کردند و دیدند که بازیکن بازکننده امتیاز 59 را کسب کرد، هند پس از برنده شدن در قرعه‌کشی و فرستادن تیم کلاه سیاه برای ضربه زدن، چهار توپ دیگر را در این اینینگ از دست داد. تام بلاندل، بازیکن پشت دروازه، که در امتیاز 49 در منطقه گالی توپ را رها کرد، در نهایت با کسب امتیاز 89 بهترین امتیاز تیمش را به دست آورد.

United Fidelity Bank was closed by US regulators on Friday in the nation’s biggest bank failure in more than two ​years, with First Citizens Bank buying the lender’s assets.

The Office ‌of the Comptroller of the Currency said Indiana-based United Fidelity was in an “unsafe or unsound condition” and likely unable to pay its obligations, handing control ​of the bank to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp to ​wind it down.

North Carolina-based First Citizens, a wholly owned subsidiary ⁠of First Citizens BancShares, agreed to buy all of the ​failed lender’s loans and most of its deposits and assets, First Citizens ​and the FDIC said.

The purchase covers assets of $5.9 billion, deposits of $4.5 billion and loans of $3.1 billion, based on United Fidelity’s balances as of Sept. 30.

It ​is the biggest US bank failure since Philadelphia-based Republic Bank ​closed in April 2024 with $6 billion in assets, according to FDIC data.

The cost to ‌the ⁠federal Deposit Insurance Fund related to the failure will be $1.83 billion, the FDIC estimated.

Reuters could not reach United Fidelity for comment outside regular business hours.

First Citizens said it was chosen through a competitive bidding ​process, with its ​bid including an ⁠asset discount of approximately $2.6 billion and no deposit premium.

United Fidelity’s depositors will automatically become First Citizens depositors, “so ​customers do not need to change their banking ​relationship and ⁠will retain all of their funds and deposit insurance coverage,” the FDIC said.

First Citizens acquires 20 bank branches in Indiana, Illinois, Colorado and ⁠Florida, ​and 2 in the US Virgin Islands.

The deal also includes United Fidelity’s subsidiaries, including its real estate development and management ​unit, Pedcor Homes.
news.content: پوشش بیشتر ما را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. United Fidelity Bank در روز جمعه توسط قانونگذاران ایالات متحده در بزرگترین ورشکستگی بانک کشور در بیش از دو سال گذشته بسته شد و First Citizens Bank دارایی های وام دهنده را خریداری کرد. دفتر کنترل ارز گفت که United Fidelity مستقر در ایندیانا در «وضعیت ناامن یا نامناسب» قرار دارد و احتمالاً قادر به پرداخت تعهدات خود نیست و کنترل بانک را به شرکت بیمه سپرده فدرال واگذار کرده تا آن را منحل کند. First Citizens و FDIC گفتند که First Citizens مستقر در کارولینای شمالی، یک زیرمجموعه کاملاً متعلق به First Citizens BancShares، با خرید تمام وام های وام دهنده شکست خورده و بیشتر سپرده ها و دارایی های آن موافقت کرد. این خرید شامل دارایی های 5.9 میلیارد دلاری 5.5 میلیارد دلاری و 5.5 میلیارد دلاری است. موجودی Fidelity از 30 سپتامبر. طبق داده‌های FDIC، این بزرگترین ورشکستگی بانک ایالات متحده از زمان تعطیلی بانک ریپابلیک مستقر در فیلادلفیا در آوریل 2024 با 6 میلیارد دلار دارایی است. FDIC برآورد کرده است که هزینه صندوق بیمه سپرده فدرال مربوط به این شکست 1.83 میلیارد دلار خواهد بود. First Citizens گفت که این شرکت از طریق یک فرآیند مناقصه رقابتی انتخاب شده است، با پیشنهاد آن شامل تخفیف دارایی تقریباً 2.6 میلیارد دلار و بدون حق بیمه سپرده گذاری.

news.originalContent:
Eisenkot struggles to form a government as talks with Netanyahu stall over rotation deal and coalition compromises.

The future of Israel’s government remains unclear following October elections that produced no clear winner.

The leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, and his main rival, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, have been convening for rounds of talks in a bid to establish a “unity government”.

But the talks ended on Sunday without a conclusive deal, with the two parties announcing that a “follow-up” meeting will be held soon.

So, what is the latest on the talks? And what happens if they fail to reach an agreement?

Following the October 27 general election, Israeli President Isaac Herzog held consultations with political parties to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority. Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats between them, while Netanyahu’s alliance won 53.

Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu.

In November, Eisenkot was instructed by Israel’s president to form a new government by December 6, with a deadline that can be extended by 14 days.

In order to form a government, one party, alliance or coalition requires a minimum 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. This means Eisenkot must ally with other parties or lawmakers to make up the seat numbers.

Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats in the election. But Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with them, which would have given him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.

He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.

Until this week, Eisenkot had struck firm coalition deals with only the Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu, bringing his total to 36 seats out of a potential 48 – still far from any majority.

Eisenkot has, therefore, been talking to Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party in hopes of establishing a unity government, but Likud wants a rotation deal that would go against Eisenkot’s promise to replace Netanyahu.

The talks have caused other complications as well. The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot this week in protest at the prospect of Netanyahu’s party remaining in government.

On Tuesday, the Yashar party announced that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with the Yisrael Beiteinu party, after meeting with leader Avigdor Lieberman, marking the first confirmed alliance since the election.

Israeli media also reported on Friday that Netanyahu is “preparing” to announce that he is willing to serve second in a prime minister rotation with Eisenkot under a unity government deal.

Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported that the offer had already been proposed unofficially, so Likud could assume “plausible deniability”, as the party remains conflicted on the terms of the offer.

The rotation deal would mean that Eisenkot would serve for the first two years as prime minister, and Netanyahu would serve the final two years.

But in a statement on Friday, Eisenkot accused the Likud party of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections. He claimed that Likud was “unwilling to compromise, and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table”.

Eisenkot said the two sides are “approaching a moment of decision”, but the question is “whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall”.

Meanwhile, Eisenkot is grappling with division among his own side as the options of forging alliances with ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority parties, who are willing to back him, have proved controversial.

The Arab-led parties could give Yashar 19 seats, but Lieberman has said he will not support any government that includes those parties.

Eisenkot said Likud’s negotiating team had refused to meet more frequently over the past two weeks. The two sides have met five times.

He added that their team was uncooperative and had rejected three proposals, including one for a state inquiry into the “failures” of October 7, the removal of “extremists” from government and a law making military or national service mandatory for all.

Instead, Eisenkot claimed that Likud proposed “the worst” proposal for a unity government with “the same government, the same partners, no change, no conscription law”.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s strategy is to “run down the clock until the mandate expires”, attempting to “drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government”.

“I do not intend to cooperate with such a charade,” he added.

One of Eisenkot’s options is to reach a deal with the country’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas. But if talks with them fail, analysts say Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between keeping Netanyahu in office or accepting support from the Arab-led parties.

The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, holds 11 seats in the Knesset, while Ra’am holds eight.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that if this were to happen, Eisenkot could tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

Analysts say that if Eisenkot reaches his deadline of December 6 to form a government without a decision, Israeli President Herzog could assign the task to another member of the Knesset, including Netanyahu, and give them a 28-day period to form a government with no extensions.

If still no government is formed, Israel could move towards a new round of elections, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a government is formed.

This happened in 2019, after the April election, when Netanyahu was unable to form a government. As a result, the Knesset was dissolved and a second election took place in September that year. Again, no majority was reached, leading to a third vote in March 2020. A government was finally formed later that month when Netanyahu struck a unity government deal with Benny Gantz’s Blue and White alliance.

news.originalContent:
Patients and health workers pay a staggering cost as war and a failing health system collide with a deadly virus.

On July 21, 2026, Emily Vandamme, a doctor with Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), was getting ready to enter the suspect ward, the small building that houses patients with suspected Ebola who are awaiting their test results. It was the second week of the Belgian physician’s month-long field mission with the Elikya Ebola treatment centre in Bunia, the largest city of the Ituri province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Because all possible Ebola cases go through this process, the small building often holds some of the most critically ill patients in the entire facility. The exhausted night team had just been forced to leave the ward after more than an hour inside. Their masks were soaked with sweat, and their goggles were so fogged that they could not safely care for patients.

Vandamme knew a woman inside who had just given birth and was bleeding out fast, but she could not rush into the ward. Entering the red zone, where infectious patients are isolated, requires a meticulous dressing ritual in which safety and focus are paramount. So, despite urgent calls coming from inside the treatment area, Vandamme had to remain completely calm while putting on her protective gear, which resembled a spacesuit. Every layer had to be checked, and she needed to hydrate and be disinfected, a process that takes at least 15 minutes. Rushing leads to mistakes, and around Ebola, a single misstep can be deadly.

When she finally entered along with her Congolese colleague, Daniel Lomonobo Anigiza, she found the woman in shock and covered in blood. Agitated and barely aware of her surroundings, the patient reached for the medical workers, who had to stop her from tearing their suits or pulling off their masks.

“Luckily, I’m quite tall, so she couldn’t reach my face,” Vandamme said.

Another heavily pregnant woman and her 17-month-old son, Bahati Prince, were in good shape but had watched the scene in horror. Next to them were three other patients, all in critical condition owing to a severe drop in blood sugar, a common complication in advanced Ebola cases.

“We were two doctors, facing four emergencies at once,” Emily recalled, speaking anxiously and in great detail, as though reliving every moment. Because there was only room for two people to put on their protective gear in the buffer room, they had to face the mayhem that day, at least initially, on their own.

While Daniel attended to the sugar-deprived patients, Emily tried to stabilise the new mother and insert an intravenous drip. Her newborn daughter was bundled up on a chair in the corner. When reinforcements finally arrived, a midwife and a nurse took over the mother’s care and Emily was able to turn her attention to the baby.

“I was afraid to look, but to my surprise she was warm and pink, doing amazingly well,” she said.

Vandamme cradled the little girl to keep her warm, while trying to arrange an urgent transfer to another hospital, hoping it would give her a fighting chance. There, she might be able to receive an experimental Ebola treatment as part of a clinical trial. At that time, only five babies in similar circumstances were known to have survived Ebola, an MSF gynaecologist had informed her.

Emily urged the team outside the ward to prepare an ambulance.

“Just as I walk back into the room with her newborn baby, the mom passes away,” she said. “Her name was Mave …”

But there was no time for mourning.

“All we could think was: ‘We’ve lost the mother, but we have to do everything we can to save her baby'. ”

Before they could act, one of the three patients with low blood sugar suddenly collapsed and died. Moments earlier, the young man had been eating and walking around, seemingly revived by a dose of glucose.

Vandamme was still holding the newborn, desperately looking for someone to take her. Fortunately, a home nurse who had already survived Ebola — and was thus largely immune — arrived. The woman often stayed in the clinic to care for the infected children.

By then, Vandamme was covered in blood and was told by the team outside to exit and be disinfected. As she made her way toward the exit, breathing heavily through the saturated mask and barely seeing through her goggles, she noticed the pregnant woman, the mother of Bahati Prince, weeping frantically.

The young man who had just died had collapsed in front of her. Now, out of nowhere, her son's condition had taken a turn for the worse. She was clutching the barely responsive toddler, begging Vandamme to help.

Despite the risk, Vandamme could not bring herself to abandon them. She asked a nurse to disinfect her bloodstained sleeves inside the red zone, then managed to insert an IV with lifesaving glucose and fluids into the boy. Slowly, he began to respond, and Vandamme rushed to the exit.

“Once we were outside, my coworkers and I just stared at each other blankly, trying to grasp what we just had witnessed,” she said.

They were all completely worn out, but the ordeal was far from over.

That same day, Vandamme went back in for two more difficult shifts, checking on Prince whenever she could. The little boy tested positive for Ebola, but surprisingly, his mother was negative. Despite the increased risk of infection amid her advanced pregnancy, she refused to leave her son’s side.

“In the days after, she was a stellar caretaker,” Emily explained. “She guarded his IV like a lioness and constantly tried to get him to eat and drink, although he could barely swallow.”

Gradually, the little boy recovered, and a few days after the crisis, he sat upright. Some food was staying in his tummy, and he even tried to play. When Vandamme saw them through the window, the mother smiled and waved proudly.

Then Prince’s mom had to be transferred to another clinic to give birth. When Vandamme arrived for her morning shift, the doctor she was relieving assured her the boy was still going strong. She was euphoric — finally a glimmer of hope. She headed straight to his room, eager to witness the miracle with her own eyes.

Instead of finding him upright and playing, however, she found Prince in his bed, lifeless and alone. Presumably, he had died from a sudden drop in blood sugar. Whether his mom’s constant care and feeding could have saved him is a question that Vandamme said would haunt her.

“Ebola is horrifically ruthless,” she said softly. “I never asked how his mother’s delivery went. At that moment, ignorance was bliss.”

The story of Bahati Prince lays bare the merciless unpredictability of Ebola. Since his death this summer in the DRC, the epidemic there has continued to spiral out of control.

More than 11,000 infections and 5,300 deaths have been recorded, meaning nearly half of those infected have died. MSF reported on November 12 that nearly two-thirds of reported Ebola-related deaths over the previous month were in communities, not in treatment centres.

That means the surveillance network, supposedly the cornerstone of an Ebola response, is blind to the majority of infections. People are dying in their homes surrounded by their families, seeding the next wave of the virus.

This is the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever to hit Congo and the second worst worldwide. Only the epidemic that swept through West Africa between 2014 and 2016 was more devastating, claiming more than 11,000 lives, according to the World Health Organization.

Three different viruses are known to cause large Ebola outbreaks: Ebola virus, also known as Zaire Ebola virus, Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus. A fourth, Tai Forest virus, can also cause Ebola disease in humans, but only one confirmed human case has been documented. Approved vaccines and virus-specific treatments are available only for Ebola virus; candidates for Sudan and Bundibugyo viruses are still under development.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccine or treatment exists. Clinical trials have recently begun using Ervebo, a vaccine proven effective against the more common Zaire strain, while researchers work frantically to develop a vaccine specifically for Bundibugyo.

Since the outbreak was first detected in May in Ituri province, the virus has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces. Experts believe the virus may have been circulating as early as February in Ituri, an active war zone with armed militias and massive refugee flows. The outbreak is now particularly difficult to contain, partly because the virus was able to circulate undetected for months.

Fears of a regional spread are growing. The virus has already crossed borders, with cases reported in Uganda, Kenya and as far away as Nigeria. With infections recorded in East, Central and West Africa, it has become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in the continent’s history, according to Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya.

A new, highly volatile virus strain colliding with the relentless “forever war” of recurring fighting in eastern DRC is an epidemiological nightmare — and one of the reasons this epidemic became the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history.

On November 6 , a tragedy occurred in the troubled North Kivu province that laid bare how the violence is undermining efforts to contain the epidemic.

About 50km west of the city of Beni, armed men raided the village of Cantine in the dark of night, killing dozens of residents with guns and machetes. According to authorities and civil society groups, at least 33 people were murdered and more than 50 houses set on fire.

The attackers also started a fire near a health post during their overnight assault, forcing around 180 patients to flee the hospital in terror. Among them were numerous suspected Ebola cases and at least one confirmed case.

Gunfire and arson forced a concentrated cluster of high-risk, unmonitored individuals to scatter out into the open and vanish. It shows how the security context in DRC can disrupt tracking and further fuel transmission.

Local authorities have blamed the attack on the ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group the Allied Democratic Forces, or ADF, rather than M23, a Rwanda-backed rebel group fighting the government. Since the M23 drove the Congolese army out of cities such as Goma and Bukavu in early 2025, the ongoing war in eastern Congo has again made international headlines.

While this latest offensive has intensified the fighting and displaced millions of people, M23 is just one of roughly 100 armed groups operating across the eastern provinces of the DRC. Many of the militias are entangled in overlapping conflicts that have plagued the region since the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

The eastern provinces of Ituri and North and South Kivu are scarred by armed conflict fuelled by ethnic tensions, struggles for political power and competition over resources. The provinces’ vast mineral wealth attracts armed groups and feeds international supply chains involving Western and Chinese companies. Investigations have linked parts of the trade to conflict financing and serious human rights abuses. In this powder keg, the Congolese state itself is a belligerent actor. UN investigators have linked the Congolese army and allied militias to numerous atrocities.

This seemingly endless war is entering its fourth decade, keeping millions of civilians trapped in anarchy. Since 1996, the conflict in the eastern part of the DRC has claimed an estimated six million lives, either by bullets or indirect effects, making it one of the deadliest conflicts in modern history. More than five million people are currently displaced across these three provinces. In rural areas, what little remained of the state has all but collapsed.

For people living amid this violence, Ebola is another threat.

“The people here live in poverty and insecurity; every day is a struggle to survive,” said Congolese physician Alex Bonane Murutsi, who works at the Ebola treatment centre in Bunia where Vandamme did her field assignment. Murutsi started working in the MSF Ebola response after contracting the deadly Bundibugyo virus and fighting for his life for 18 days earlier this year.

“The epidemic makes their already difficult life even harder. For many, it’s hard to accept the prevention measures,” he said.

He has seen families resist safe burials and Ebola survivors face exclusion and stigma. Funerals traditionally involve a lot of touching, dancing around and washing the body of the deceased — rituals that are important to the local culture. Safe burials require isolating the body in a sealed bag to prevent viral transmission. Distrust in Ebola response workers and the inability to perform the traditional rites and say a proper farewell cause some families to hide deaths or resist safe burials.

As for survivors’ stigma, local populations do not always understand that recovered patients are no longer infectious, leading to fear and avoidance due to a lack of public information or misinformation. Even health workers can get a hard time from their own families, Murutsi explained, because they don’t always understand how they can safely work in a treatment centre.

“In the beginning, there was not enough communication. People didn’t always understand why certain measures were necessary,” he explained.

That mistrust sometimes turns violent. One of the soft-spoken doctor’s colleagues was working at a rural health post when a patient suffering from severe bleeding was brought in. The medical staff voiced their suspicion of Ebola, which infuriated the patient’s companions. They insisted the disease did not exist in their village and accused the health workers of bringing it there. The doctor was assaulted and had to flee.

But Dr Murutsi stresses that medical teams do not face hostility everywhere. In Bunia, there is more trust, partly because local health workers engage directly with the community.

“People know us and we take the time to explain why certain measures are important. You don’t earn people’s trust by simply telling them what to do; you have to talk to them,” he explained.

Anna Halford is acutely aware of the challenges of fighting Ebola in conditions of insecurity. The British aid worker coordinates MSF’s response to the outbreak across the DRC.

“The physical access to some of the affected areas is severely compromised,” she said. “This makes it extremely difficult to transport supplies and establish proper screening and surveillance.”

In some conflict-affected areas, violence and insecurity prevent health teams from reaching communities, leaving sick people with little or no access to Ebola testing and care. This also hampers contact tracing, which is crucial for fighting the virus. For every confirmed case, teams must quickly identify people who may have been exposed and monitor them for three weeks after their last known contact.

Halford, an experienced humanitarian who also helped tackle the largest-ever West African Ebola outbreak, emphasised that violence is not the only obstacle to taming the virus.

“Several areas not affected by armed groups are also seeing a rise in cases and struggling with the response,” she pointed out.

Supply routes are not only cut off by the risk of attacks, but also by the country’s weak infrastructure. Patients often have to travel for hours along bumpy roads to reach a treatment centre. Meanwhile, medicines and medical supplies often fail to reach remote villages in good condition.

This leaves front line health workers across the whole DRC without the basic protective equipment needed to safely treat suspected Ebola patients. Halford recently encountered this in a remote clinic far from the conflict-ridden East.

“In an area where, thankfully, numbers are still low, medical workers were forced to make do with makeshift protective gear designed for COVID-19 and flip-flops,” she said, expressing her frustration.

Responding to Ebola is an inherently complex and costly operation. According to the veteran field worker, the security risks act as a disease multiplier, further exacerbated by the crippling lack of funding that Congolese health services historically struggled with.

This longstanding problem has only grown worse in recent years, since international donations have sharply declined. Last year, the United Nations’ humanitarian emergency response plan for the Congo was funded by barely a quarter of the required amount.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who led the US response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and now heads Refugees International, argued on the Zeteo media website that the dismantling of USAID played a role in the delayed detection. The US Agency for International Development (USAID) previously deployed rapid response teams, known as DART, to detect and contain outbreaks.

With them gone, the early warning system failed, allowing the virus to circulate undetected from February through May. According to him, the cuts also contributed to shortages of protective equipment and limited the capacity to analyse samples and conduct tests.

The collapse of USAID hit even harder because other donors — such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Canada — cut back on aid almost simultaneously, according to epidemiologist Alain Casseus, head of the infectious diseases division of the leading medical charity Partners in Health.

As a result, the Congolese Ministry of Health and Africa CDC were initially left largely on their own to tackle the raging epidemic with limited staff and supplies.

The fragile Congolese healthcare system was quickly overwhelmed.

Early Ebola symptoms resemble those of malaria or typhoid, and infections were often misidentified in understaffed and poorly equipped health centres. After the outbreak was officially declared in May, it took months to bring the testing capacity up to the required level.

Halford is relieved that the international community has recently stepped up efforts to close the funding gap. In September, new pledges from G20 foreign ministers and major donors brought total global commitments since May to around $2.9bn.

“I’m delighted that there have been some donors, and the Congolese state itself, which have pledged and disbursed resources,” she said. “But for whatever reason, we are not seeing enough of the effect of those resources on the ground.”

That mismatch is apparently so striking that Javid Abdelmoneim, the international president of MSF, sounded the alarm earlier this month. In a scathing statement, he warned that the funds simply have not reached the front lines of the fight against Ebola.

“Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many front-line responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets,” Abdelmomein said in an MSF statement.

“Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.”

Abdelmomein cites cases of untrained and unpaid health workers, ambulances unable to respond due to lack of fuel and phantom surveillance teams that exist on spreadsheets but are nowhere to be seen in the field.

Despite funding earmarked for this crucial work, a comprehensive system to detect infections and trace contacts is still lacking, Abdelmomein said.

“In Ituri, only nine percent of patients with Ebola disease treated by our teams had previously been identified as contacts by the surveillance system,” Abdelmomein added.

Halford, his coworker, claims there’s a serious lack of oversight of how pledged funds reach operations on the ground. But according to her, there’s no single explanation or culprit to point fingers at.

“This is not a criticism directed at the DRC government, which itself denounced that lack of transparency. Poor planning and oversight lead to many overlapping aid projects in one area, while others are left neglected,” she said.

Halford notes that the specific circumstances in DRC, where one of the deadliest viruses in the world strikes in a war-torn region with a historically weak health system, make an already difficult Ebola response extremely hard.

“Tackling Ebola requires everything, everywhere, all at once. It’s an uphill battle, but it is a collective responsibility to overcome these challenges in order to stop this devastating virus,” she added.

As devastating as Ebola is for those infected, fighting the disease takes an equally gruelling toll on health workers. What happened to Prince shows how quickly a hard-won victory can turn into tragedy.

At Elikya, the intense human suffering medical staff faced every day wore them out emotionally. The thick protective suits they had to wear inside the isolation tents pushed them to their physical limits. That centre was closed on October 31 because MSF redeployed teams and resources to other affected areas with greater needs, with other treatment facilities absorbing Elikya’s patients. Murutsi is still working on the Ebola response, conducting fieldwork near Isiro, the capital of Haut-Uele province.

The Ebola virus is not airborne but spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids. Doctors and nurses entering the red zone must therefore wear heavy water-repellent suits that cover their entire bodies, along with FFP2 masks, goggles and at least two pairs of rubber gloves.

Vandamme described how the heat became unbearable the moment the suit was put on and how her goggles fogged up within minutes. The thick gloves left her with barely any sense of touch, turning routine procedures such as inserting an IV or cutting an umbilical cord into painstakingly frustrating tasks.

“You have to conserve your energy constantly, or you won’t be able to function properly. You fall back on experience and established routine,” she said. In these conditions, health workers can stay inside for no more than 90 minutes. Their masks are soaked with sweat by that time, giving the virus a possible entry point. Besides, breathing becomes increasingly difficult and exhaustion raises the risk of mistakes.

“Often you want to deal with just one more emergency, but you can barely think straight and your protective gear is no longer safe. You have to put your own safety first. That’s especially difficult when there aren’t enough colleagues to take over,” Emily said. “In that one hour, you witness things as an emergency physician you might not see in an entire month elsewhere.”

There is barely any time for a comforting word or a hug. To terrified Ebola patients, the health workers seem like faceless beings in yellow hazmat suits who suddenly appear and quickly vanish.

The emotional distance was the hardest part of her mission, the Belgian doctor said. “Normally, I try to spend some time with patients, hold their hand or simply talk about something else for a moment.”

But at Elikya, “everything had to be done as quickly and efficiently as possible”.

The lack of human connection also weighs heavily on the patients, especially children. But Elikya, which means “hope” in Lingala [Bantu language], was named that for a reason.

“Some children arrive completely alone, having lost almost their entire families,” Murutsi said. “That is why we introduced a system in which Ebola survivors help care for other patients.”

Survivors have developed antibodies against the virus and are mostly protected against reinfection. Some voluntarily return to isolation wards as gardes-malades, or caregivers. They comfort orphaned children by acting as surrogate parents. They wash patients too weak to wash themselves, or simply keep them company. They provide the human warmth and attention that overburdened medical staff cannot provide.

Murutsi explained that this innovation was introduced in Elikya for the first time during the current outbreak.

“They are indispensable in the paediatric ward,” said Murutsi. “They give children who would otherwise be completely alone the care and affection they desperately need.”

For Vandamme, who worked alongside Murutsi in Bunia, the gardes-malades show just how crucial it is to include the local communities in the struggle against Ebola. During her summer stint at Elikya, she saw how they made a huge difference for the many children she cared for who lost their entire family.

Five children she treated lay beside their parents as the father or mother died vomiting and bleeding.

“Some children just kept lying next to their dead parent, holding them, refusing to let go. Ebola leaves so many children orphaned,” she said.

The Belgian doctor was no stranger to human suffering before her stint in DRC. Last year, Vandamme worked in the emergency room of Al-Aqsa Hospital in Gaza and before that amid Haiti's extreme gang violence in Port-au-Prince.

“Yet this was by far my most intense assignment,” she said. “Never before had I seen so many people die in a single day who I’d seen alive just hours earlier.”

But besides overwhelming grief, Emily also witnessed remarkable resilience at Elikya. One patient who embodied that was Ruth, a 40-year-old grandmother admitted in mid-July with her two grandsons, aged three and six.

Their parents had both died at home, presumably from Ebola.

The youngest boy was critically ill and died within two days. “Ruth knew she might lose her entire family, so we did everything we could to save his older brother,” Emily said.

But the boy soon stopped eating and drinking.

“We couldn't tell whether it was the disease or the grief of losing his little brother, who had died right beside him.”

Ruth was devastated when he died too, but she forced herself to eat and drink rehydration fluids. Then we learned that back home, a third grandchild still needed her care, a three-month-old baby. She simply refused to let the grief overwhelm her.

“A few days later, I walked past her tent. She gave me a thumbs-up and said, ‘Merci beaucoup'.”

Vandamme was visibly moved by the memory.

“We hadn’t been able to save her two grandsons, yet she was still grateful to us. If this epidemic is to be defeated, such selfless resilience will undoubtedly have played a part.”
news.content: بیماران و کارکنان بخش سلامت، در شرایطی که جنگ و یک سیستم سلامت ناکارآمد با یک ویروس کشنده در هم می‌آمیزند، هزینه‌ای سرسام‌آور می‌پردازند. در 21 ژوئیه 2026، امیلی واندام، پزشکی از سازمان پزشکان بدون مرز (MSF)، آماده می‌شد تا وارد بخش مشکوک شود، ساختمان کوچکی که بیماران مشکوک به ابولا در آن بستری هستند و منتظر نتایج آزمایش خود هستند. این دومین هفته از مأموریت میدانی یک‌ماهه پزشک بلژیکی در مرکز درمان ابولا الیکیا در بونیا، بزرگترین شهر استان ایتوری در شرق جمهوری دموکراتیک کنگو بود. از آنجا که همه موارد احتمالی ابولا این فرآیند را طی می‌کنند، این ساختمان کوچک اغلب برخی از بیمارانی را در خود جای می‌دهد که وضعیت وخیم‌تری در کل مرکز دارند. تیم شیفت شب که کاملاً خسته بودند، مجبور شده بودند پس از بیش از یک ساعت حضور در بخش، آنجا را ترک کنند. ماسک‌های آنها خیس عرق شده بود و عینک‌هایشان آنقدر بخار گرفته بود که نمی‌توانستند به طور ایمن از بیماران مراقبت کنند. واندام زنی را در داخل می‌شناخت که تازه زایمان کرده بود و خونریزی شدیدی داشت، اما نمی‌توانست با عجله وارد بخش شود. ورود به منطقه قرمز، جایی که بیماران عفونی در آن قرنطینه می‌شوند، مستلزم یک فرآیند دقیق پوشیدن لباس است که در آن ایمنی و تمرکز از اهمیت بالایی برخوردار است. بنابراین، علیرغم تماس‌های فوری که از داخل منطقه درمان می‌آمد، واندام مجبور بود هنگام پوشیدن لباس محافظ خود که شبیه لباس فضانوردی بود، کاملاً آرام بماند. هر لایه باید بررسی می‌شد و او نیاز داشت که مایعات بنوشد و ضدعفونی شود، فرآیندی که حداقل 15 دقیقه طول می‌کشد. عجله کردن منجر به اشتباه می‌شود و در اطراف

news.originalContent:
Socialist PM Pedro Sanchez seeks re-election but polls have suggested conservative PP and far-right Vox could reach threshold for majority.

Spain faces political shift as far right gains ground

Madrid, Spain – Voters in Spain are set to head to the polls in an election that could open the door to the far right entering the country’s national government, half a century after the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.

After a bitter campaign largely focused on housing and immigration, Sunday’s snap vote pits two sharply different accounts of socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s eight years in power against each other. One says the country has become a bastion of social progress and a driver of economic growth in a largely stagnant Europe. The other, embraced by the opposition conservatives and the far right, says Spain needs a profound change after years of alleged corruption and opportunism.

“They [the elections] have been framed in plebiscitary terms, as a vote for or against Pedro Sanchez’s leadership,” Alvaro Sanchez-Garcia, a political scientist and postdoctoral fellow at Spain’s Centre for Political and Constitutional Studies, told Al Jazeera. In a campaign this polarising, he said, voters who switch parties tend to stay within the same bloc, with only a few crossing from left to right or the other way around.

Polls suggest the conservative People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party – projected to finish third – to secure the 176 seats required for an outright majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Most surveys suggest the PP and Vox would reach that number together, giving PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo a path to power through either a coalition or a minority government backed by Vox in parliament.

Despite the unfavourable predictions, Sanchez has expressed optimism that left-leaning voters will mobilise in large numbers come election day to prevent a right-wing surge. In 2023, his PSOE had finished second but Sanchez secured another term with support from parties to his left, and Catalan and Basque groupings.

“I can’t conceive of us losing,” he said in a radio interview on Friday, before addressing supporters at his final campaign rally in the capital, Madrid: “This election about one thing only: Whether Spain moves forward or goes backwards.”

In power since 2018, Sanchez says Spain has never been in a better shape, pointing to the dynamism of the country’s economy. The European Commission forecasts growth of 2.6 percent for Spain this year, compared with 1.2 percent for the eurozone.

Sanchez has become a popular figure among Europe’s progressives at a time of a wider shift to the right across the European Union. The 54-year-old has frequently clashed with US President Donald Trump, refused to increase defence spending to 5 percent as requested by other NATO members and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide.

But at home, not everyone sees him the same way. “People abroad think he is a hero, but not here,” said Isabel Labayen, a longtime PP voter. “How is it possible that we are praised abroad but people [in Spain] can’t afford a house, food or have doctor appointments in months rather than days?” the 64-year-old asked. “We have a problem.”

Housing was also what brought the election forward. Sanchez called the snap vote in October after parliament rejected two measures intended to protect renters following protests over high housing costs and evictions.

Opponents say Sanchez’s moments on the world stage have failed to translate into better living conditions for people in Spain. “You can’t eat GDP,” Feijoo told the prime minister during a televised debate last week.

Critics also say the economic indicators might have indeed improved, but this was mostly driven by the absorption of foreign labour; the minimum wage has increased, but average salaries have remained the same; and services feel increasingly stretched as foreign-born residents have grown by more than four million since the PSOE took power in 2018.

Sanchez’s reputation has also been tarnished by corruption cases involving his inner circle and family, the handling of a migration crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta earlier this year and two deadly train crashes a few months apart that provided the opposition with ammunition to attack the government for overseeing a failed state that very much needs repairing.

This has energised Vox, which has become a rising political force in recent years. Campaigning on giving Spaniards “national priority” – a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits – and banning mass regularisation of migration, the far-right party is predicted to make the biggest gains compared with the other major parties. In 2023, it secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress; it is now set to double that, capturing about 18 percent of the national vote.

“We’re governed by a criminal mafia, led by an unscrupulous boss who knows no bounds when it comes to lying,” Vox leader Santiago Abascal told supporters at his last rally, held inside a bullring in Valencia, on Friday.

Feijoo has previously said he would prefer the PP to rule on its own, with Vox supporting it in parliament, rather than forming a joint governing coalition. That will depend on numbers: should the far-right party make major gains, it will have stronger leverage in any negotiations.

Yolanda Roman, the global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, said the prospect of a PP-Vox coalition seems to frighten voters less than it did in 2023. That could make it harder for the Socialists to rally voters by warning them about the far right entering government. “I see less fear,” she said, “or maybe we have come to terms with the idea that this is happening.”

The two parties already govern together in four regions, including the former socialist stronghold of Andalusia. Judging by what Vox has demanded of the PP in regional negotiations, Sanchez-Garcia said, a strong result on Sunday could embolden it to ask for key ministries.

Polling stations will open at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT). Official provisional results will start trickling in straight away, with the overall picture expected to be clear before midnight.
news.content:
نخست وزیر سوسیالیست پدرو سانچز به دنبال انتخاب مجدد است اما نظرسنجی ها نشان می دهد که حزب محافظه کار PP و راست افراطی Vox می توانند به آستانه اکثریت برسند. اسپانیا با تغییر سیاسی روبرو است زیرا راست افراطی به میدان می رسد.
مادرید، اسپانیا – رای دهندگان در اسپانیا قرار است در انتخاباتی به پای صندوق های رای بروند که نیم قرن پس از پایان دیکتاتوری فرانسیسکو فرانکو می تواند راه را برای ورود راست افراطی به دولت ملی این کشور باز کند. پس از یک کمپین تلخ که عمدتاً بر مسکن و مهاجرت متمرکز شده بود، رای فوری روز یکشنبه دو روایت کاملاً متفاوت از هشت سال سلطنت پدرو سانچز، نخست وزیر سوسیالیست را در مقابل یکدیگر قرار داد. یکی می گوید این کشور به سنگر پیشرفت اجتماعی و محرک رشد اقتصادی در اروپای عمدتاً راکد تبدیل شده است. دیگری که توسط محافظه‌کاران اپوزیسیون و راست افراطی پذیرفته شده است، می‌گوید که اسپانیا پس از سال‌ها فساد و فرصت‌طلبی ادعایی به یک تغییر عمیق نیاز دارد. آلوارو سانچز-گارسیا، یک متخصص سیاسی و متخصص علوم سیاسی و متخصص علوم سیاسی در Spaadoindoin و متخصص علوم سیاسی در Spaadoindoin، آن‌ها [انتخابات] در قالب همه‌پرسی، به عنوان رأی موافق یا مخالف رهبری پدرو سانچز تنظیم شده‌اند. مطالعات، به الجزیره گفت. او گفت در کمپینی که این دوقطبی است، رای دهندگانی که احزاب را تغییر می دهند، تمایل دارند در همان بلوک باقی بمانند، و تنها تعداد کمی از چپ به راست یا برعکس عبور می کنند. نظرسنجی ها نشان می دهد که حزب محافظه کار خلق (PP) اکثر کرسی ها را به دست خواهد آورد اما به حزب راست افراطی Vox - که پیش بینی می شود سوم شود - نیاز دارد تا 1 را تضمین کند.

news.originalContent:
Baghdad’s push to seize control of smuggling routes, border crossings and oilfields has Washington’s support.

United States President Donald Trump has thrown his weight behind Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s campaign against oil smuggling. Baghdad has moved to take control of border crossings and oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region and has confronted Kataib Hezbollah, Iran’s most powerful armed ally in Iraq.

The endorsement came days before talks between Baghdad and Erbil are due to take place on December 1 under the sponsorship of the head of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council.

It has prompted Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser ⁠to Iran’s Supreme Leader ⁠Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, to warn Iraq not to become a “tool ⁠of Trump” ⁠in an X post on Saturday.

In a post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump wrote: “We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.

“We support Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions,” he added.

The post marked Washington’s first comment on tensions between Baghdad and Erbil. On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region’s border crossings and several oilfields under federal control. On Wednesday, Iraq’s top court ruled that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all of the country’s international borders, including those of the Kurdish region. On Thursday, Iraq closed two crossings in the region, one with Syria and one with Iran.

Salim Zakhour, a researcher specialising in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera that the timing is significant, as Trump’s post comes after Baghdad’s measures and before the planned dialogue meeting.

“It is a clear message, first to the federal government, as a show of support for it,” he said. “But the more important message is for the authorities and Kurdish leaders in the Kurdistan region. It tells them that all the measures taken by the federal government have strong American backing.”

The Iraqi government says it wants to clamp down on oil smugglingو which is harming its economy.

The campaign began in Jurf al-Sakhar, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a town in Babil province south of Baghdad. The armed group Kataib Hezbollah has held the town since 2014, when Iran-backed groups took it from ISIL (ISIS), and its mostly Sunni residents were displaced.

Senior Iraqi security, army, police and oil officials told the Reuters news agency that Kataib Hezbollah has since run an oil smuggling network there, siphoning off state-owned crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.

Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed and referred to the courts. Kataib Hezbollah, which the US designates as a “terrorist” organisation, denies the allegations.

Al-Zaidi gave the group until November 20 to leave the town. A day before the deadline, the two sides reached a compromise, reportedly following direct intervention by Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s Quds Force.

Under the deal, government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar and set up a joint operations centre. Kataib Hezbollah units are due to withdraw gradually as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) units deploy in phases.

Kataib Hezbollah is not the only group resisting Baghdad’s push to bring weapons under state control. Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have also refused to disarm. After the armed groups missed a September 30 deadline to hand over their weapons to the state, the government pushed the deadline to June 2027.

Baghdad then extended the campaign to the Kurdish region. Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that Iraq has lost an estimated $100bn between 2008 and 2025 from oil smuggled through the region. Reuters reported that it was unclear how that figure had been calculated.

Kurdish region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called the measures unconstitutional and rejected them outright. Thousands of Kurds protested on Thursday, although Kurdish officials have said they do not want clashes with Baghdad and have left the door open to talks.

Liqaa Makki, a senior researcher at the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, said Baghdad turned to the Kurdish region before the Jurf al-Sakhar operation was finished.

“The forces went in, but what next? There were promises that residents would return, that the town would be rebuilt and that Kataib Hezbollah would leave. None of that has happened,” he said.

Makki said al-Zaidi was responding to Shia armed groups asking why Baghdad was targeting them and not the Kurds, and wanted to show them “I am tough with everyone.”

He added that the prime minister could exploit divisions within the Kurdish region between the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, based in Sulaimaniyah, and Erbil. “This is a good opportunity, because Sulaimaniyah is with him against Erbil,” he said.

Ghalib al-Daami, an academic and political researcher in Baghdad, told Al Jazeera that the Federal Supreme Court has already settled the legal question about borders with the Kurdish region.

“The border crossings, in terms of control, are run by the federal government, which also sets fiscal policy, but the actual day-to-day management of the crossings is to be joint,” he said. That would mean federal forces working alongside local Kurdish forces, such as the Asayish and the police.

“Oil, as interpreted by the Federal Court and the Iraqi constitution, is the property of all Iraqis,” he added.

“Very,” Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “It is Iran’s main land outlet under blockade.”

Seloom said Iraqi buyers imported about $11.9bn of Iranian goods in 2024, one-fifth of Iran’s non-oil exports. “Gas for Iraqi power plants adds $4-5bn a year, and Iraqi banks give Tehran a route around sanctions,” he said.

Iraq is one of Iran’s most important economic partners. Bilateral trade topped $10bn in 2025, according to Iraqi official figures, driven mainly by Iranian exports of food and consumer goods. Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization put the figure at about $11.6bn.

Energy is at the centre of the relationship. According to US Energy Information Administration data, Iranian gas fuels power plants that produce 30 to 40 percent of Iraq’s electricity.

Iraq has also served as a channel for Iran to get around sanctions. Reuters revealed in late 2024 that a fuel oil smuggling network in Iraq was generating at least $1bn a year for Iran and its allies.

That channel has become more valuable as pressure on Tehran has grown amid the US war. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports used for exporting oil and has threatened sanctions against countries and groups that continue doing business with Iran.

Washington also has unusual leverage over Baghdad because Iraq’s oil revenues are held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In April, the US halted a $500m cash payment to Iraq to press Baghdad to take action against Iran-backed groups.

Seloom said the best-documented scheme involves Iranian oil that is relabelled as Iraqi. “US Treasury designations since July 2025 describe blending and forged papers, and in May the trail reached Iraq’s deputy oil minister,” he said.

He said a newer claim – that crude from Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah is trucked into Iran – “rests on one intelligence document that AFP has viewed without being able to confirm, and Erbil rejects it.”

An Iraqi intelligence document cited by the state news agency INA suggests crude is being moved by tanker truck from oilfields in Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah provinces into Iran. There, it is reportedly blended with Iranian oil and sent on to Afghanistan, in what the document describes as an effort to help Iran “evade sanctions”. The document also suggests there may be a second route via crossings into Turkiye.

Washington has made similar accusations for some time. In May, the US Department of the Treasury sanctioned Iraq’s deputy oil minister, Ali Maarij al-Bahadly, accusing him of abusing his position to divert oil for the benefit of Iran and its allied armed groups in Iraq. Earlier, the Treasury sanctioned a network of companies run by Iraqi businessman Salim Ahmed Said. It accused the network of blending Iranian oil with Iraqi oil and selling it as purely Iraqi.

Seloom said Iraq is “the land gap” in Trump’s blockade of Iran.

“Closing it costs him no troops,” he said. “The crackdown slots into Washington’s economic-blockade strategy. It also squeezes militia funding and shores up al-Zaidi.”

The security source in Baghdad told the AFP news agency that the crackdown has US backing as Washington seeks to limit Iran’s economy.

In an X post on Saturday, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser ⁠to Iran’s Supreme Leader ⁠Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, warned Iraq not to become a “tool ⁠of Trump” ⁠after media reports that Iraq ⁠had closed ⁠several crossings ⁠following US efforts to blockade Iran’s ‌land borders.

He wrote: “In the geometry of our foreign policy, sharing a common destiny with our neighbours is a fundamental principle. In the darkest days, Iran stood by the people of Iraq with all its might and proved its friendship. This unbreakable bond requires Baghdad to remain vigilant on border issues so that it does not become a tool in the hands of the enemies of Islam and an instrument for carrying out the policies of the criminal Trump.”

Zakhour said the US position on the Kurds has also shifted. Washington backed Kurdish autonomy for decades, from the no-fly zones of the 1990s to the decentralised federal system written into the 2005 constitution.

“Now there is a different approach, led by the US envoy to Iraq and Syria, Ambassador Tom Barrack,” he said. “This approach is towards more centralised decision-making, both in general and especially on investment and oil.”

He said Barrack’s view is that “when American companies sign contracts, there must be a single party to sign with, and there must be no disputes after the signing.

“Everything we are seeing now is aimed at securing that demand,” Zakhour added.

Makki said Washington’s backing has freed al-Zaidi to take on Erbil. “America is now standing behind him with all its strength,” he said. “So he is not afraid that the Americans will side with the Kurds. On the contrary, they are asking the Kurds to stand with al-Zaidi.”

Al-Daami rejected any suggestion that US backing compromises al-Zaidi, who has steered Iraq closer to Washington and whom Trump hosted at the White House in July this year.

“Fighting corruption, preventing smuggling and controlling national wealth are clearly a domestic agenda,” he said. “Yes, that agenda lines up with the American one.”

“Yes, but more as a launchpad than a battlefield,” Seloom said. “Militia participation in any renewed US-Iran round is very likely.”

He said Iraq has had no US troops present since September 30. “So I expect militia fire from Iraqi soil and US air strikes on militia leaders, not a ground war,” he said.

The risk is rising. The US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, and a ceasefire took effect following a memorandum of understanding in June. But that agreement, which would have paved the way to wider peace talks, fell apart, and the two sides have continued to exchange attacks in recent weeks, while the US blockades Iranian ports.

Trump has said he “would not hesitate” to resume full military strikes if diplomacy fails, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the US escalates.

Iraq has already been drawn in. Since the war began, several Iraqi armed groups have pledged to support Iran’s war effort, and Baghdad has acknowledged that attacks on neighbouring countries have been launched from its territory. In July, joint US-Saudi strikes on PMF sites across Iraq killed at least 20 of its members.

Baghdad is trying to stay out of any new round of US-Iran fighting. In a phone call with Trump on November 5, al-Zaidi said Iraq would not allow its territory to be used to attack neighbouring countries. Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein warned Iraqi armed groups against joining any Iranian retaliation. “Pushing Iraqi society into the war will lead to a disaster,” he told Dijlah TV.

Al-Daami said outside powers would inevitably shape the outcome. “The foreign actor, whether we like it or not, has influence in the Middle East and in Iraq,” he said.

The dispute with Erbil carries its own economic stakes for Baghdad. Zakhour warned that if Baghdad centralises control over oil, the Kurdish region’s budget “will depend entirely on transfers from the Baghdad government”.

Al-Daami predicted the talks would end with the Kurdish government accepting the court’s ruling. “In the end, the disputes between the two governments will result in the federal government controlling all of its border crossings and all of its territory,” he said.
news.content: تلاش بغداد برای به دست گرفتن کنترل مسیرهای قاچاق، گذرگاه‌های مرزی و میادین نفتی از حمایت واشنگتن برخوردار است. دونالد ترامپ، رئیس‌جمهور ایالات متحده، از کمپین علی الزیدی، نخست‌وزیر عراق علیه قاچاق نفت حمایت کرده است. بغداد برای کنترل گذرگاه های مرزی و میادین نفتی در منطقه نیمه خودمختار کردستان حرکت کرده و با کتائب حزب الله، قدرتمندترین متحد مسلح ایران در عراق مقابله کرده است. این تایید چند روز پیش از برگزاری مذاکرات بین بغداد و اربیل در اول دسامبر با حمایت رئیس شورای عالی قضایی عراق صورت گرفت. این تایید باعث شد که محمد مخبر، مشاور رهبر ایران آیت‌الله مجتبی خامنه‌ای، به ترامپ هشدار دهد که در روز شنبه به ترامپ منصوب نشود. ترامپ روز جمعه در پستی در Truth Social نوشت: «ما از تلاش‌های نخست‌وزیر عراق علی الزیدی برای اعمال قدرت دولتی در سراسر عراق، توقف قاچاق نفت عراق، پایان دادن به فساد و قرار دادن تمام سلاح‌ها تحت کنترل انحصاری دولت حمایت می‌کنیم.» او افزود: «ما از تلاش‌های نخست‌وزیر الزیدی برای ایجاد عراقی واحد، موفق، موفق و قوی حمایت می‌کنیم.» این پست اولین اظهار نظر واشنگتن در مورد تنش بین بغداد و اربیل بود. روز سه شنبه، الزیدی حرکت کرد تا گذرگاه های مرزی اقلیم کردستان و چندین میدان نفتی را تحت کنترل فدرال قرار دهد. روز چهارشنبه، دادگاه عالی عراق حکم داد که بغداد می تواند نیروهای فدرال را در تمام نقاط بین المللی این کشور مستقر کند.
